T1.objective: Primary hypothesis: SIMD masks validate UTF-8 constraints across the whole buffer, unlike T2's ASCII-span locator. Explore block classification, shifted continuation requirements, restricted second-byte checks, cross-block state, and a bounded tail. Compare relevant SIMD variants only when supported by the frozen target and unchanged build; do not alter flags or add runtime environment probing. Keep the supplied scalar implementation as a control, and report any useful hybrid as a distinct variant rather than excluding it. Preserve exact scalar-value validation, ABI, output, and thread budget. Use the official mixed-width n=65536 timing for performance and official ASCII/malformed checks for correctness, paying particular attention to vector boundaries and truncations where covered. Record failed variants.
T1.subject: Whole-stream SIMD UTF-8 validation with cross-block state

T2.objective: Primary hypothesis: vector high-bit scans can skip ASCII spans while the existing strict scalar decoder handles non-ASCII code points. The benefit depends on the actual official mixed-width input containing useful ASCII spans; do not assume this or use synthetic-only results as evidence for the scored workload. Start decoding at a known code-point boundary and treat the first high-bit byte as input to validate—not as an assumed lead, since it may be a stray continuation. Keep loads and tails within n. Preserve exact validity, ABI, output, and thread budget. Measure the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and run the official ASCII/malformed correctness checks, especially for boundaries. Report this approach separately from T1's whole-buffer validation; label any hybrid distinctly and record failed variants.
T2.subject: SIMD-assisted ASCII-run skipping with a scalar slow path

T3.objective: Primary hypothesis: reducing scalar decoding control flow or dependencies helps the mixed-width workload; the supplied baseline already has an ASCII fast path, so do not assume ASCII scanning is the only scalar cost. Compare the baseline decoder with compact-state/DFA or reduced-branch scalar variants, measuring each under the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and checking official ASCII/malformed correctness. Keep scalar decoding as the focus, but do not treat that focus as a ban on useful correctness-preserving experiments; label any hybrid separately from pure-scalar results. Preserve exact validity, ABI, output, bounds, and thread budget. Report failed variants.
T3.subject: Branch-reduced scalar UTF-8 decoding

Gm1.objective: Starting from the fastest correct source 31112, retain its 16-byte SSE2 ASCII-prefix scan and test replacing its scalar suffix with T1's measured 8-byte ASCII-word/mixed-block decoder from 1bef. This tests whether skipping ASCII blocks after the first non-ASCII block helps without sacrificing the faster prefix. Preserve all correctness and protocol constraints; remeasure the combined program and do not assume additive gains.
Gm1.stop_condition: Reject the integration on any correctness failure or if its official mixed-width mean is not faster than 39.98 µs.
Gm1.subject: Test a faster ASCII-prefix scan with a word-scanned scalar suffix

mission.hypothesis: This distinct hybrid tests whether SIMD can capture later ASCII spans without paying for a SIMD restart after each decoded code point: skip complete 16-byte ASCII vectors, then strictly decode a 64-byte window after a mixed vector before resuming SIMD. It may help if the official mixed-width input has later ASCII spans; otherwise the scalar windows may add overhead. The fallback begins at a code-point boundary and validates the first high-bit byte rather than assuming it is a lead. No speedup is claimed.

retained: Added a strict single-code-point scalar decoder and used it for scalar validation, preserving UTF-8 checks for overlong encodings, surrogates, out-of-range code points, and malformed continuations.

Skipped only complete 16-byte vectors whose bytes are all ASCII; after a mixed vector, decoded a scalar window through at least 64 bytes before resuming SIMD at the resulting known code-point boundary.
Kept vector loads within length, delegated the tail to scalar validation, and preserved the run ABI and output.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: This distinct hybrid tests whether SIMD can capture later ASCII spans without paying for a SIMD restart after each decoded code point: skip complete 16-byte ASCII vectors, then strictly decode a 64-byte window after a mixed vector before resuming SIMD. It may help if the official mixed-width input has later ASCII spans; otherwise the scalar windows may add overhead. The fallback begins at a code-point boundary and validates the first high-bit byte rather than assuming it is a lead. No speedup is claimed.

retained: Added a strict single-code-point scalar decoder and used it for scalar validation, preserving UTF-8 checks for overlong encodings, surrogates, out-of-range code points, and malformed continuations.

Skipped only complete 16-byte vectors whose bytes are all ASCII; after a mixed vector, decoded a scalar window through at least 64 bytes before resuming SIMD at the resulting known code-point boundary.
Kept vector loads within length, delegated the tail to scalar validation, and preserved the run ABI and output.

mission.hypothesis: This remains a one-way 16-byte SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix hybrid, not T1-style whole-buffer validation. The selected parent locates the first high-bit lane in a mixed vector before calling the scalar decoder. Since that vector starts at a known code-point boundary and the scalar decoder already skips ASCII, starting it at the vector boundary may avoid the mask-shifting lane search at the cost of rechecking at most 15 ASCII bytes. The first high-bit byte remains input to strict validation, including when it is a stray continuation. Prior timings motivate the contrast but do not establish its cause; measure on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and official ASCII/malformed boundary checks.

retained: Remove the bit-by-bit search for the first high-bit lane; when a complete 16-byte SIMD block contains any high bit, invoke the strict scalar decoder from that block's known code-point boundary.
Skip only complete 16-byte blocks confirmed entirely ASCII; leave tails within n to the scalar decoder and retain exact UTF-8 validity behavior, ABI, output, and thread budget.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: This remains a one-way 16-byte SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix hybrid, not T1-style whole-buffer validation. The selected parent locates the first high-bit lane in a mixed vector before calling the scalar decoder. Since that vector starts at a known code-point boundary and the scalar decoder already skips ASCII, starting it at the vector boundary may avoid the mask-shifting lane search at the cost of rechecking at most 15 ASCII bytes. The first high-bit byte remains input to strict validation, including when it is a stray continuation. Prior timings motivate the contrast but do not establish its cause; measure on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and official ASCII/malformed boundary checks.

retained: Remove the bit-by-bit search for the first high-bit lane; when a complete 16-byte SIMD block contains any high bit, invoke the strict scalar decoder from that block's known code-point boundary.
Skip only complete 16-byte blocks confirmed entirely ASCII; leave tails within n to the scalar decoder and retain exact UTF-8 validity behavior, ABI, output, and thread budget.

mission.hypothesis: A bounded one-way SSE2 scan of complete 16-byte blocks may improve on the prior prefix hybrid by locating the first high-bit lane within the first mixed block and starting the strict scalar decoder there, avoiding its scan of preceding ASCII bytes. All skipped bytes are ASCII, so this remains a known code-point boundary; the high-bit byte itself is still validated by the scalar decoder. The effect is input-dependent and must be measured on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload.

retained: Extracted the existing strict scalar UTF-8 decoder into a helper used for the suffix and for builds without SSE2.
Added a bounded SSE2 scan over complete 16-byte blocks, skipping only blocks whose high-bit mask is zero.
For the first mixed block, located the first high-bit byte and handed that byte and the remaining suffix to strict scalar validation; bounded vector loads and tail handling by length.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A bounded one-way SSE2 scan of complete 16-byte blocks may improve on the prior prefix hybrid by locating the first high-bit lane within the first mixed block and starting the strict scalar decoder there, avoiding its scan of preceding ASCII bytes. All skipped bytes are ASCII, so this remains a known code-point boundary; the high-bit byte itself is still validated by the scalar decoder. The effect is input-dependent and must be measured on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload.

retained: Extracted the existing strict scalar UTF-8 decoder into a helper used for the suffix and for builds without SSE2.
Added a bounded SSE2 scan over complete 16-byte blocks, skipping only blocks whose high-bit mask is zero.
For the first mixed block, located the first high-bit byte and handed that byte and the remaining suffix to strict scalar validation; bounded vector loads and tail handling by length.

mission.hypothesis: A one-way SSE2 scan over complete 32-byte ASCII blocks, followed by the strict scalar decoder from the first non-ASCII block boundary, may balance the measured 16-byte and 64-byte prefix variants. This tests an intermediate block size on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload; it does not assume that input has useful ASCII spans or claim a speedup.

retained: Replace the parent's repeated 64-byte scan inside the decoder loop with a one-way scan of complete 32-byte blocks at the known initial code-point boundary.
Skip a block only when both bounded 16-byte SSE2 loads contain no high-bit bytes; on the first block with a high bit, retain its start index for strict scalar validation of the suffix.
Retain scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, run ABI, output, and thread budget.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A one-way SSE2 scan over complete 32-byte ASCII blocks, followed by the strict scalar decoder from the first non-ASCII block boundary, may balance the measured 16-byte and 64-byte prefix variants. This tests an intermediate block size on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload; it does not assume that input has useful ASCII spans or claim a speedup.

retained: Replace the parent's repeated 64-byte scan inside the decoder loop with a one-way scan of complete 32-byte blocks at the known initial code-point boundary.
Skip a block only when both bounded 16-byte SSE2 loads contain no high-bit bytes; on the first block with a high bit, retain its start index for strict scalar validation of the suffix.
Retain scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, run ABI, output, and thread budget.

mission.hypothesis: A portable 8-byte SWAR bit-plane classifier may reduce per-byte control flow on mixed-width inputs by classifying lead and continuation lanes together, comparing shifted continuation requirements, and checking restricted second-byte ranges. If a sequence crosses a block boundary, defer that block and suffix to the strict scalar validator instead of carrying state. This contrasts with the selected T1 parent's ASCII-block skip and the earlier carry-state variants; it is an unmeasured experiment, not a claimed speedup.

retained: Retained the strict scalar UTF-8 validator as the correctness control and bounded suffix validator.
Added portable 8-byte SWAR bit-plane extraction and lead/continuation classification without alignment assumptions or target-specific instructions.
Compared shifted continuation requirements per block and checked E0, ED, F0, and F4 second-byte restrictions.
Delegated from a block boundary to the scalar validator whenever continuation requirements cross that boundary; kept the run ABI, output, and thread budget unchanged.

This contrasts with the selected T1 parent's ASCII-block skip and the earlier carry-state variants; it is an unmeasured experiment, not a claimed speedup.

mission.hypothesis: A repeated 32-byte SSE2 ASCII-skip hybrid may reduce scan-loop overhead relative to the selected parent's 16-byte scan while retaining scalar UTF-8 decoding. Whether 32-byte scans help the official mixed-width n=65536 workload remains unmeasured.

retained: Changed the repeated ASCII scan from one 16-byte vector per iteration to two adjacent 16-byte vectors checked together; scan only when at least 32 bytes remain.

Retained bounded scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, ABI, output, and thread budget.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A repeated 32-byte SSE2 ASCII-skip hybrid may reduce scan-loop overhead relative to the selected parent's 16-byte scan while retaining scalar UTF-8 decoding. This tests a different block granularity, not T1-style whole-buffer validation. Catalog evidence is mixed: the selected 16-byte repeated-scan parent measured 60.43 µs, while a distinct one-way 16-byte SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix program measured 39.98 µs against the 49.62 µs baseline. Whether 32-byte scans help the official mixed-width n=65536 workload remains unmeasured.

retained: Changed the repeated ASCII scan from one 16-byte vector per iteration to two adjacent 16-byte vectors checked together; scan only when at least 32 bytes remain.
Skip a 32-byte block only when the OR-combined vectors have no high bits. Otherwise leave the index unchanged for scalar scanning and strict decoding from the known boundary.
Retained bounded scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, ABI, output, and thread budget.

mission.hypothesis: Baseline T3 measurements put the original decoder at 49.623 µs and predicate aggregation at 49.545 µs, while the measured shared-loop and table-DFA variants were slower. This distinct pure-scalar test replaces per-width validation branches in the main loop with masked predicates and arithmetic width advancement, using a bounded four-byte lookahead and the scalar decoder for the final short tail. It may reduce control-flow dependencies, but redundant lookahead loads for short sequences may erase any gain; the controller must measure it on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload.

retained: Keep the scalar ASCII-run skip and the existing run ABI and output assignment.
For non-ASCII bytes with at least four bytes remaining, use bounded lookahead loads and bitwise-masked continuation and UTF-8 boundary predicates instead of width-specific validation branches.
Advance by an arithmetically derived sequence width and use an explicit bounds-checked scalar decoder for the short tail.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: Baseline T3 measurements put the original decoder at 49.623 µs and predicate aggregation at 49.545 µs, while the measured shared-loop and table-DFA variants were slower. This distinct pure-scalar test replaces per-width validation branches in the main loop with masked predicates and arithmetic width advancement, using a bounded four-byte lookahead and the scalar decoder for the final short tail. It may reduce control-flow dependencies, but redundant lookahead loads for short sequences may erase any gain; the controller must measure it on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload.

retained: Keep the scalar ASCII-run skip and the existing run ABI and output assignment.
For non-ASCII bytes with at least four bytes remaining, use bounded lookahead loads and bitwise-masked continuation and UTF-8 boundary predicates instead of width-specific validation branches.
Advance by an arithmetically derived sequence width and use an explicit bounds-checked scalar decoder for the short tail.

mission.hypothesis: A portable 64-bit high-bit mask can skip complete ASCII blocks throughout the buffer. For mixed blocks, scalar-decode through the block boundary and any crossing code point, avoiding both repeated per-byte ASCII checks and the prior full bit-plane classifier's boundary bookkeeping. This hybrid may help when complete ASCII blocks occur often; dense mixed-width data may instead pay the mask-check overhead.

retained: Retained the supplied scalar UTF-8 validator as validate_utf8_scalar.
Added a portable 64-bit high-bit test, loaded with memcpy, to skip complete ASCII blocks without alignment or endianness assumptions.
For mixed blocks, decoded scalar code points through the block boundary so sequences crossing it are validated once without carried state.
Used the scalar validator for the bounded tail and preserved the run ABI and output.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A portable 64-bit high-bit mask can skip complete ASCII blocks throughout the buffer. For mixed blocks, scalar-decode through the block boundary and any crossing code point, avoiding both repeated per-byte ASCII checks and the prior full bit-plane classifier's boundary bookkeeping. This hybrid may help when complete ASCII blocks occur often; dense mixed-width data may instead pay the mask-check overhead.

retained: Retained the supplied scalar UTF-8 validator as validate_utf8_scalar.
Added a portable 64-bit high-bit test, loaded with memcpy, to skip complete ASCII blocks without alignment or endianness assumptions.
For mixed blocks, decoded scalar code points through the block boundary so sequences crossing it are validated once without carried state.
Used the scalar validator for the bounded tail and preserved the run ABI and output.

mission.hypothesis: The prior lead-directed and shared-loop scalar variants measured slower than baseline, while predicate aggregation was valid and very close to baseline; these results do not establish that branch reduction helps. This pure-scalar experiment uses byte classes and a compact transition table to replace width-specific decoding branches while retaining an ASCII-run fast path. It tests whether simpler transitions outweigh the class/transition lookup dependencies. A prior DFA development attempt failed correctness, so this version explicitly represents restricted second-byte classes; performance remains unmeasured.

retained: Replaced scalar width-specific decoding with a byte-class table and compact transition table, including distinct continuation subranges for restricted second-byte validation.
Retained an ASCII-run fast path while state is accepting; rejected invalid transitions immediately and rejected incomplete sequences at end of input.
Preserved the existing run ABI and output assignment.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: The prior lead-directed and shared-loop scalar variants measured slower than baseline, while predicate aggregation was valid and very close to baseline; these results do not establish that branch reduction helps. This pure-scalar experiment uses byte classes and a compact transition table to replace width-specific decoding branches while retaining an ASCII-run fast path. It tests whether simpler transitions outweigh the class/transition lookup dependencies. A prior DFA development attempt failed correctness, so this version explicitly represents restricted second-byte classes; performance remains unmeasured.

retained: Replaced scalar width-specific decoding with a byte-class table and compact transition table, including distinct continuation subranges for restricted second-byte validation.
Retained an ASCII-run fast path while state is accepting; rejected invalid transitions immediately and rejected incomplete sequences at end of input.
Preserved the existing run ABI and output assignment.

mission.hypothesis: A one-way SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix hybrid using bounded 64-byte ASCII blocks may amortize scan overhead versus the earlier 16-byte prefix hybrid. It skips a block only when all four SSE2 vectors are ASCII; otherwise the strict scalar decoder resumes at that block's known code-point boundary and validates the first high-bit byte rather than assuming it is a lead. Whether this granularity helps the official mixed-width n=65536 workload is unmeasured.

retained: Replace repeated SIMD scans between decoded code points with a single bounded scan over complete 64-byte prefix blocks, each checked by four unaligned SSE2 loads.
Skip a 64-byte block only when all bytes are ASCII; otherwise leave the index at the block start for strict scalar validation of the suffix, including any leading ASCII and the first high-bit byte.
Retain scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity behavior, run ABI, output, and thread budget.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A one-way SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix hybrid using bounded 64-byte ASCII blocks may amortize scan overhead versus the earlier 16-byte prefix hybrid. It skips a block only when all four SSE2 vectors are ASCII; otherwise the strict scalar decoder resumes at that block's known code-point boundary and validates the first high-bit byte rather than assuming it is a lead. Whether this granularity helps the official mixed-width n=65536 workload is unmeasured.

retained: Replace repeated SIMD scans between decoded code points with a single bounded scan over complete 64-byte prefix blocks, each checked by four unaligned SSE2 loads.
Skip a 64-byte block only when all bytes are ASCII; otherwise leave the index at the block start for strict scalar validation of the suffix, including any leading ASCII and the first high-bit byte.
Retain scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity behavior, run ABI, output, and thread budget.

mission.hypothesis: The selected lead-directed decoder was valid but measured slower than baseline, while predicate aggregation was valid and near baseline speed; neither result establishes the cause. This pure-scalar variant tests whether deriving the continuation count from lead comparisons and sharing a continuation loop reduces the width-specific control flow. The extra loop and boundary checks may instead cost more, so controller measurement is needed.

retained: Retain the ASCII-run fast path and the existing ABI and output behavior.
Replace separate width-specific continuation validation with a continuation count derived from lead-byte comparisons and a shared loop.
Check the remaining length before continuation loads and preserve the E0, ED, F0, and F4 second-byte restrictions.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: The selected lead-directed decoder was valid but measured slower than baseline, while predicate aggregation was valid and near baseline speed; neither result establishes the cause. This pure-scalar variant tests whether deriving the continuation count from lead comparisons and sharing a continuation loop reduces the width-specific control flow. The extra loop and boundary checks may instead cost more, so controller measurement is needed.

retained: Retain the ASCII-run fast path and the existing ABI and output behavior.
Replace separate width-specific continuation validation with a continuation count derived from lead-byte comparisons and a shared loop.
Check the remaining length before continuation loads and preserve the E0, ED, F0, and F4 second-byte restrictions.

mission.hypothesis: The catalog has three distinct, valid SIMD-scan programs and no repeats, but none beat the 49.62 µs baseline: the 16-byte scan measured 60.43 µs, the selected lane-bisection parent 77.82 µs, and the 64-byte variant 81.00 µs. This contrasting SIMD-prefix/scalar-remainder hybrid tests whether repeatedly restarting SIMD scans and locating a lane after each decoded code point costs more than it saves. It skips only complete 16-byte ASCII vectors; on the first vector containing any high bit, it sends the suffix from that block boundary to the strict scalar decoder. This avoids assuming the high-bit byte is a lead and preserves bounded loads, but gives up SIMD scanning of later ASCII runs. Measure it on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload; do not infer a speedup from synthetic inputs.

retained: Replaced repeated SIMD scans interleaved with scalar code-point decoding with a bounded SIMD prefix scan over complete 16-byte blocks.

On the first vector with high-bit bytes, call the strict scalar validator on the suffix beginning at that vector's known code-point boundary; the scalar decoder validates any leading ASCII and treats the first high-bit byte as input to validate.
Retained scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, run ABI, output, and thread budget.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: The catalog has three distinct, valid SIMD-scan programs and no repeats, but none beat the 49.62 µs baseline: the 16-byte scan measured 60.43 µs, the selected lane-bisection parent 77.82 µs, and the 64-byte variant 81.00 µs. This contrasting SIMD-prefix/scalar-remainder hybrid tests whether repeatedly restarting SIMD scans and locating a lane after each decoded code point costs more than it saves. It skips only complete 16-byte ASCII vectors; on the first vector containing any high bit, it sends the suffix from that block boundary to the strict scalar decoder. This avoids assuming the high-bit byte is a lead and preserves bounded loads, but gives up SIMD scanning of later ASCII runs. Measure it on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload; do not infer a speedup from synthetic inputs.

retained: Replaced repeated SIMD scans interleaved with scalar code-point decoding with a bounded SIMD prefix scan over complete 16-byte blocks.

On the first vector with high-bit bytes, call the strict scalar validator on the suffix beginning at that vector's known code-point boundary; the scalar decoder validates any leading ASCII and treats the first high-bit byte as input to validate.
Retained scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, run ABI, output, and thread budget.

mission.hypothesis: The baseline and previous lead-directed candidate retain the same general scalar width dispatch, but the latter was slower. This pure-scalar variant tests whether aggregating per-sequence validity predicates with bitwise OR, rather than short-circuit OR, reduces control-flow or dependency overhead on mixed-width input. It keeps the ASCII scan and checks remaining length before every continuation-byte load. The compiler may produce equivalent code or the extra predicate work may outweigh any benefit; performance is unmeasured.

retained: Keep the scalar ASCII-run fast path and existing width-specific decoding structure.
After each width-specific bounds check, load the required continuation bytes and combine all continuation and lead-boundary predicates using non-short-circuit bitwise OR.
Use remaining-length checks before continuation-byte reads to retain safe bounds behavior for all input lengths.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: The baseline and previous lead-directed candidate retain the same general scalar width dispatch, but the latter was slower. This pure-scalar variant tests whether aggregating per-sequence validity predicates with bitwise OR, rather than short-circuit OR, reduces control-flow or dependency overhead on mixed-width input. It keeps the ASCII scan and checks remaining length before every continuation-byte load. The compiler may produce equivalent code or the extra predicate work may outweigh any benefit; performance is unmeasured.

retained: Keep the scalar ASCII-run fast path and existing width-specific decoding structure.
After each width-specific bounds check, load the required continuation bytes and combine all continuation and lead-boundary predicates using non-short-circuit bitwise OR.
Use remaining-length checks before continuation-byte reads to retain safe bounds behavior for all input lengths.

mission.hypothesis: A guarded SSE2 scan that checks four adjacent 16-byte vectors as one 64-byte ASCII superblock may amortize scan-loop overhead relative to earlier 16-byte scans on long ASCII spans. If any byte in a superblock has its high bit set, the unchanged scalar scanner finds and validates it, including stray continuation bytes. The official mixed-width n=65536 workload must determine whether larger blocks help or merely add overhead.

retained: Added a compile-time-guarded SSE2 scan that loads four 16-byte vectors only when at least 64 bytes remain, combines them to test whether the full 64-byte block is ASCII, and skips the block only when every byte is ASCII.
Retained scalar ASCII scanning, strict UTF-8 decoding, scalar tail handling, ABI, output, and thread budget.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A guarded SSE2 scan that checks four adjacent 16-byte vectors as one 64-byte ASCII superblock may amortize scan-loop overhead relative to earlier 16-byte scans on long ASCII spans. If any byte in a superblock has its high bit set, the unchanged scalar scanner finds and validates it, including stray continuation bytes. The official mixed-width n=65536 workload must determine whether larger blocks help or merely add overhead.

retained: Added a compile-time-guarded SSE2 scan that loads four 16-byte vectors only when at least 64 bytes remain, combines them to test whether the full 64-byte block is ASCII, and skips the block only when every byte is ASCII.
Retained scalar ASCII scanning, strict UTF-8 decoding, scalar tail handling, ABI, output, and thread budget.

mission.hypothesis: This distinct T2 variant tests whether locating the first high-bit lane from the SIMD mask is cheaper than the parent’s scalar byte-by-byte scan of a mixed 16-byte block. SIMD still skips only complete ASCII blocks; the first high-bit byte, including a possible stray continuation, is passed to the existing strict scalar decoder. Loads remain bounded by n. It is not T1 whole-buffer validation or a hybrid; the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and ASCII/malformed boundary checks must determine whether it helps.

retained: In the existing SSE2 ASCII-run scanner, use a four-step binary subdivision of the movemask to return the first high-bit lane directly instead of falling back to byte-by-byte source scanning within that vector block.
Leave the strict scalar UTF-8 decoder, scalar tail handling, ABI, output, and thread budget unchanged.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A lead-directed scalar decoder may reduce the per-byte table lookups and state-dependent transitions of the supplied DFA on mixed-width input by validating continuation bytes directly per code point, while retaining the ASCII-run fast path. This may instead lose from its lead-classification branches; controller measurement is needed.

retained: Replace the byte-class and DFA transition tables with direct lead-range classification and continuation-byte checks grouped by UTF-8 sequence length.
Retain the ASCII-run scan and validate E0/ED and F0/F4 boundary restrictions explicitly.
Check remaining input length before each continuation-byte read to preserve bounds and malformed-input rejection.

mission.hypothesis: A compile-time-guarded SSE2 scan can skip complete 16-byte ASCII blocks before the existing scalar UTF-8 decoder handles non-ASCII bytes. This may reduce per-byte work on long ASCII spans, but the benefit depends on the official mixed-width input; the first high-bit byte remains for scalar validation. The baseline is valid at 49.623 µs mean, but no candidate speedup is established.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A compile-time-guarded SSE2 scan can skip complete 16-byte ASCII blocks before the existing scalar UTF-8 decoder handles non-ASCII bytes. This may reduce per-byte work on long ASCII spans, but the benefit depends on the official mixed-width input; the first high-bit byte remains for scalar validation. The baseline is valid at 49.623 µs mean, but no candidate speedup is established.

retained: Added a compile-time-guarded SSE2 high-bit scan that advances across full 16-byte ASCII blocks only; scalar scanning handles tails and the first block containing a high-bit byte before the unchanged strict decoder validates it.

mission.hypothesis: A safer hybrid may retain the throughput benefit of portable 8-byte bit-mask validation for complete blocks while avoiding fragile carried boundary state: when a block may end inside a code point, validate that block and the remaining suffix with the supplied scalar control. This tests whole-block classification and constraint masks while preserving scalar handling for boundary cases.

retained: Preserved the supplied scalar UTF-8 validator as a correctness control and suffix fallback.
Used portable 64-bit word classification to validate fully contained 8-byte blocks, including continuation placement and restricted second-byte constraints.
When valid prefix masks indicate a sequence may cross a block boundary, delegated validation from that block through the end to the scalar control instead of carrying pending/range state.
Retained a scalar bounded-tail path for remaining bytes.

model_interpretation.hypothesis: A safer hybrid may retain the throughput benefit of portable 8-byte bit-mask validation for complete blocks while avoiding fragile carried boundary state: when a block may end inside a code point, validate that block and the remaining suffix with the supplied scalar control. This tests whole-block classification and constraint masks while preserving scalar handling for boundary cases.

retained: Preserved the supplied scalar UTF-8 validator as a correctness control and suffix fallback.
Used portable 64-bit word classification to validate fully contained 8-byte blocks, including continuation placement and restricted second-byte constraints.
When valid prefix masks indicate a sequence may cross a block boundary, delegated validation from that block through the end to the scalar control instead of carrying pending/range state.
Retained a scalar bounded-tail path for remaining bytes.

hypotheses.claim: Un hybride distinct (chemin SIMD pour l’ASCII, validation scalaire inchangée hors ASCII) mérite un essai, mais aucun gain n’est établi ici.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Sur la cible et avec le build figés, sans sondage d’environnement, vérifier les contrôles officiels ASCII et malformés, puis mesurer le texte mixte n=65536; inclure les frontières de blocs et troncatures lorsqu’elles sont couvertes par le protocole.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Arrêter si un contrôle échoue, ou si la moyenne des cinq répétitions de confirmation n’est pas inférieure à celle du contrôle scalaire.

observations.claim: Le contrôle scalaire est valide, avec une moyenne mesurée de 49,62 µs et un score de 0,5.
L’essai 1bef6299446e4809 est valide, mais sa moyenne mesurée (57,50 µs; score 0,4632) est supérieure à celle du contrôle scalaire.
Un autre essai a échoué à l’exécution; un développement associé est incorrect. Un développement distinct est marqué development_valid, sans mesure de performance officielle.

uncertainties: Le catalogue fourni n’affiche que les six premières entrées sur dix; les quatre suivantes et les pages détaillées de preuve/source ne sont pas visibles ici.
La couverture effective des frontières SIMD et des troncatures n’est pas établie par les éléments visibles.

hypotheses.claim: 31112ea757f04c4a mérite une confirmation : sa mesure initiale est correcte et plus rapide que le baseline, mais elle ne confirme ni la reproductibilité ni l’usage effectif du balayage SIMD.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Examiner le source puis lancer les cinq répétitions officielles sur le mixed-width n=65536 et les contrôles ASCII/malformés, notamment les continuations isolées, frontières de blocs et queues.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Arrêter si un contrôle échoue ou si la moyenne de confirmation n’est pas inférieure à celle du baseline.

hypotheses.claim: 5e2fba8baac84b46 est une variante correcte plus lente, utile provisoirement comme témoin de comparaison, pas comme candidate privilégiée.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Comparer son source et son comportement à 31112ea757f04c4a, puis mesurer les deux avec les mêmes contrôles officiels et cinq répétitions.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Ne plus poursuivre 5e2fba8baac84b46 comme candidate si un contrôle échoue ou si elle reste plus lente que le baseline à la confirmation.

observations.claim: Le baseline est enregistré valide et correct, avec une moyenne de 49,62 µs et un score de 0,5.
31112ea757f04c4a est enregistré valide et correct à 39,98 µs en moyenne (score 0,5538); 6af9a1e290384d22 l’est aussi à 49,02 µs (score 0,5031). Ce sont des mesures initiales, pas des confirmations.
Des alternatives correctes plus lentes sont mesurées : 5e2fba8baac84b46 à 60,43 µs, 0350732002f14eaa à 77,82 µs, d66449d1d846490e à 81,00 µs et cd2a550c3b714843 à 55,14 µs.

uncertainties: Les sources des variantes n’ont pas été examinées : le caractère SIMD ou hybride et la sûreté des chargements et queues restent à vérifier.
Les éléments visibles ne précisent pas le contenu exact du workload mixte, sa densité de plages ASCII ni l’étiquetage détaillé des cas de correction.
Aucune confirmation indépendante à cinq répétitions n’est visible.

hypotheses.claim: Une variante scalaire à état compact ou DFA pourrait réduire les dépendances, mais aucun résultat visible ne démontre que ce changement améliore ec1a.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Tester une variante scalaire sans hybridation sur le mélange officiel n=65536, avec cinq répétitions de confirmation et les vérifications officielles ASCII/malformé; comparer ses mesures à baseline et ec1a.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Arrêter à toute erreur de correction; ne retenir la variante que si sa moyenne de confirmation est inférieure à celles de baseline et ec1a.

hypotheses.claim: Les essais valides plus lents db2837 et e871 peuvent servir de contrôles négatifs, sans être promus comme choix de performance sur la seule base des résultats actuels.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Confirmer ces deux essais valides et ec1a avec le même protocole officiel sur n=65536, puis vérifier ASCII et malformé; comparer les moyennes de confirmation.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Arrêter à tout échec de correction; écarter db2837 ou e871 comme candidats de performance si sa moyenne confirmée n'est pas inférieure à celle d'ec1a.

observations.claim: Le baseline est mesuré valide et correct, à 4,9623157435502036e-05 s de moyenne et score 0,5.

ec1a est mesuré valide et correct, à 4,954522326594237e-05 s et score 0,5003929386010361. Son extrait montre trois échantillons de benchmark et 18 cas de correction réussis; l'écart de moyenne avec le baseline est faible.
db2837 est valide et correct, mais sa moyenne mesurée est plus élevée: 6,173383679537698e-05 s, score 0,4456222779560411.

e871 est valide et correct, mais sa moyenne mesurée est plus élevée: 5,649993401752732e-05 s, score 0,46759999879447073. Une tentative de développement, e871-h01, est incorrecte; e871-h02 est valide en développement sans mesure de performance visible.

uncertainties: Les sources des variantes ne sont pas visibles ici; leurs différences algorithmiques et leur caractère strictement scalaire ou hybride ne peuvent être établis.
Les étiquettes des patterns ne sont pas explicitées dans l'extrait de correction; il ne permet pas d'attribuer spécifiquement les 18 cas aux contrôles ASCII et malformé.
Aucun résultat de confirmation final G ni aucune page d'évidence supplémentaire n'est visible dans les éléments fournis.

contract.statement:
Optimize the supplied baseline on AMD EPYC 9654 with GCC 14.2. Use the actual AB-MCTS research trees and persistent Mother memory/integration policy.
Validate UTF-8 input1 of n bytes according to Unicode scalar-value rules (reject malformed continuations, overlong encodings, surrogates, values >0x10ffff, truncated sequences). Write uint32 1 for valid and 0 otherwise. n=65536 performance on valid mixed-width text, also ASCII and malformed correctness checks. One core. The supplied baseline contains a documented correctness repair of the historical benchmark validator.
Edit only src/candidate.cpp. Keep extern C void run(const void*input1,const void*input2,void*output,int n,int parameter,int threads). Respect the threads argument as the CPU thread budget. Inputs are read-only and 64-byte aligned. Overwrite the full specified output on every call; no cached answers, external tools or libraries, filesystem, environment inspection, timing inspection or phase detection. Ordinary C++17, OpenMP and x86 intrinsics are available. Do not modify the protected correctness or timing protocol. Scratch allocation inside run is allowed and included in timing. The harness measures native wall-clock time, excluding input generation, oracle and compilation. Search and confirmation use different seeds. Numerical tolerances are fixed. The optimized reference source is withheld. Choose topics independently, record failed attempts, complete memory integration and independently confirm final G.
